extracted.intended_audience: law students, patent attorneys, inventors, and others learning claim construction principles
extracted.subtask_description: Interpreting patent claims where a specification includes both broader and narrower claims, using the doctrine that claims should be construed to avoid rendering narrower claims redundant. Useful for claim drafting and litigation/claim-construction analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of claim differentiation
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine of claim differentiation is a principle of patent claim construction. It presumes that when a patent contains both broad and narrow claims, the broader claims are intended to cover a scope different from and wider than the narrower claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A court should generally interpret the broader claims in a way that does not make the narrower claims meaningless or superfluous. The underlying idea is that a patent applicant would not bother to include a narrower claim if it covered exactly the same ground as a broader claim. Practical effect: when construing claims, avoid reading a broad claim so narrowly that it captures the very limitation that a dependent or narrower claim explicitly adds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption against redundancy in claim drafting/interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: When a patent contains multiple claims (some broad, some narrow), assume each claim is intended to have a distinct meaning and purpose rather than being redundant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this presumption to preserve the separate scopes of broader and narrower claims. Examples provided: (1) Software — a broad 'system for managing digital media files' should not be limited to systems that categorize by AI when a narrower claim expressly recites AI categorization; (2) Pharmaceutical — a broad 'chemical compound for treating inflammation' should not be read as limited to salicylic-acid derivatives when a narrower claim names that derivative; (3) Manufacturing — a broad 'method for producing lightweight composite materials' should not be construed to only cover a UV-curing-at-specific-wavelength process when a dependent claim specifies that process. Anti-pattern: construing a broad claim so narrowly that a dependent claim becomes pointless or superfluous.
